records.old: 8 lessons × 40 minutes = 320 minutes total
records.new: 8 lessons × 80 minutes (each a double period of 2 × 40 minutes) = 640 minutes total
records.why: Every lesson is an 80-minute double period (2 × 40 minutes), so the unit total is 8 × 80 = 640 minutes, not 8 × 40 = 320. Checked by adding the eight lesson durations: 80+80+80+80+80+80+80+80 = 640.

records.old: which families do Al and Cl belong to?
records.new: which families do Al and Cl belong to? Suggested pacing for the 80-minute double period: Predict 8 min, Observe 28, Explain 28, Driving Question Board 7, Model Building 9 (the notebook copy of the model can be finished as homework).
records.group_headline: Several lessons were packed beyond their 80-minute double period; each overview now gives a suggested pacing, with the two most overloaded lessons (2 and 5) trimmed
records.why: Adding the activity times written in Lesson 2 (prediction about 8, card sort and report-back about 30, Explain parts A+B+C = 10+10+8 = 28, DQB about 8, model about 15) gives about 90 minutes or more, more than the 80 available. A pacing line tells teachers where the time goes; the sort now stops earlier to free minutes. 8+28+28+7+9 = 80.

records.old: Stop groups at the 25-minute mark.
records.new: Stop groups at the 20-minute mark.
records.why: Card sort now stops at 20 minutes so that the report-back fits inside the 28-minute Observe phase (20 + about 8 = 28).

records.old: Learners do not yet explain the puzzle fully; the unit does that.
records.new: Learners do not yet explain the puzzle fully; the unit does that. Suggested pacing for the 80-minute double period: Predict 10 min, Observe 20, Explain 20, Driving Question Board 12, Model Building 18.
records.why: Gives teachers a realistic split of the 80 minutes (10+20+20+12+18 = 80).

records.old: and to jobs such as sufuria, wire and mabati.
records.new: and to jobs such as sufuria, wire and mabati. Suggested pacing for the 80-minute double period: Predict 8 min, Observe 40 (hands-on about 25, data table about 15), Explain 18, Driving Question Board 6, Model Building 8.
records.why: The Observe phase already uses 25 + 15 = 40 minutes, so the other four phases have 40 minutes together; 8+40+18+6+8 = 80.

records.old: so we must understand it before judging where it is safe.
records.new: so we must understand it before judging where it is safe. Suggested pacing for the 80-minute double period: Predict 8 min, Observe 20, Explain 30, Driving Question Board 8, Model Building 14.
records.why: Explain holds the electron diagrams, CER, three equations and the safety card, so it needs the largest share: 8+20+30+8+14 = 80.

records.old: They add new questions to the DQB and revise the class family model.
records.new: They add new questions to the DQB and revise the class family model. Suggested pacing for the 80-minute double period: Predict 8 min, Observe 30 (two stations of 9 minutes, demonstration and pop test about 5, table and discussion about 7), Explain 24, Driving Question Board 8, Model Building 10.
records.why: Two 12-minute stations plus the demonstration, Explain and the rest added up to about 90 minutes; 8+30+24+8+10 = 80.

records.old: do Station A and Station B for 12 minutes each
records.new: do Station A and Station B for 9 minutes each
records.why: Two stations of 12 minutes (24) plus the demonstration did not fit in the Observe phase; 9 + 9 + about 12 for the demonstration, pop test and table = 30.

records.old: and reflect on caring for self and others.
records.new: and reflect on caring for self and others. Suggested pacing for the 80-minute double period: Predict 8 min, Observe 17, Explain 30 (individual writing about 12, pair swap about 5, product pitches about 13), Driving Question Board 10, Model Building 15.
records.why: Final Explanation writing and five group pitches need the most time: 8+17+30+10+15 = 80.

records.old: Guiding idea to build on: Mg has two outer electrons to lose, and the metal is denser and has a higher melting point (Lesson 3 data), so it holds on more strongly than Na and reacts less readily.
records.new: Guiding idea to build on: Mg has two outer electrons to lose, and its nucleus has 12 protons pulling on the outer shell compared with 11 in Na, so the outer electrons are held more tightly and are lost less readily than Na's one. (Density and melting point are evidence that Mg holds its atoms more strongly, not the reason.)
records.group_headline: Why magnesium is less reactive than sodium was explained by its density and melting point; it is now explained by the stronger pull of the nucleus on two outer electrons
records.reference: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Chapter 6.5 "Periodic Variations in Element Properties" (effective nuclear charge, ionisation energy)
records.why: Density and melting point do not cause reactivity; they are separate properties. In period 3, Na has 11 protons and Mg 12 pulling on the same third shell, and Mg must lose two electrons. Checked with first ionisation energies Na 496 and Mg 738 kJ/mol (and Mg needs 738 + 1451 for two electrons): Mg holds its electrons more tightly.

records.old: Magnesium has to lose 2 outer electrons rather than 1, so it loses them less readily than sodium does.
records.new: Magnesium has to lose 2 outer electrons rather than 1, and its nucleus (12 protons) pulls on them more strongly than sodium's nucleus (11 protons), so it loses them less readily than sodium does.
records.why: Keeps the Final Explanation exemplar consistent with the corrected Lesson 5 reasoning (protons 12 versus 11 in the same shell).
records.reference: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Chapter 6.5 "Periodic Variations in Element Properties"
records.where: Final Explanation, Part 3: Reactivity and position in the periodic table, exemplar

records.old: justifying each position from the evidence.
records.new: justifying each position from the evidence (calcium was not tested: the teacher gives a reference card saying calcium sinks in cold water and fizzes steadily, more slowly than sodium).
records.why: Learners are asked to justify the position of Ca from evidence, but they have never seen calcium react, so the claim would be unsupported. A short reference card gives them the evidence.

records.old: Remember Mr. Otieno's sodium fizzing across the trough on Thika Road day.
records.new: Remember Mr. Otieno's sodium fizzing across the trough in Lesson 1.
records.group_headline: Lesson 5 contained a confusing cross-reference and a claim that confused magnesium the element with magnesium compounds
records.why: "On Thika Road day" refers to nothing in Lesson 1; the sodium demonstration was in the classroom, and Thika Road is only the lamp. Cross-reference corrected.

records.old: such as flash bulbs in older cameras and in some antacid tablets
records.new: such as flash bulbs in older cameras (the metal itself) and, as compounds such as magnesium hydroxide, in some antacid medicines
records.reference: WHO ATC classification A02AA (magnesium compounds used as antacids)
records.why: Antacid tablets contain magnesium compounds, not magnesium metal; saying "magnesium is in antacids" blurs element and compound, the very distinction the unit teaches (salt versus sodium). Checked: milk of magnesia is magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2.

records.old: 'Sodium sank neither in oil nor in water; it floated. Look at the density column. Which other metals would float on water? Turn to your partner.' He cold-calls 3 pairs and asks: 'What evidence in the table supports that?' He adds: 'Notice there is no melting point row for the gases, only a boiling point. Why do you think that is?'
records.new: 'Sodium floated on water. (It sinks in paraffin oil, which has a density of about 0.8 g/cm3, so it can be stored there away from air and water.) Look at the density column. Which other metals would float on water? Turn to your partner.' He cold-calls 3 pairs and asks: 'What evidence in the table supports that?' He adds: 'Notice that for neon and argon the table gives only a boiling point. Why do you think that is?'
records.reference: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, densities of Na (0.97 g/cm3) and paraffin/kerosene (about 0.8 g/cm3)
records.why: Sodium does not float in oil: at 0.97 g/cm3 it is denser than paraffin oil (about 0.8 g/cm3), which is why it sinks and is stored under it. The prompt also said the table has no melting point for the gases, but chlorine has one (-101 C); now it refers only to neon and argon. Checked against the data table in the same lesson.

records.old: Aluminium (Al): density 2.70 g/cm3, melting point 660 C.
records.new: Aluminium (Al): density 2.70 g/cm3, melting point 660 C, conducts heat and electricity well, and is protected by a thin oxide layer that resists corrosion.
records.group_headline: The Final Explanation expected learners to use aluminium's heat conduction and oxide layer, which were not in the data given; they are now in the data and in the lessons
records.reference: OpenStax Chemistry 2e / CRC Handbook: thermal conductivity of Al about 237 W/m K; aluminium oxide passivation layer
records.why: Part 4(a) asks learners to use the data, but heat conduction and the oxide layer appeared only in the exemplar. Adding them to the data list (and to Lessons 3 and 7, where Al is first met) makes the question answerable from taught material. Audit item confirmed.

records.old: Al: 2.70 g/cm3, 660 C, conducts.
records.new: Al: 2.70 g/cm3, 660 C, conducts electricity and heat well.
records.why: Lesson 3 later credits Al's heat conduction for the sufuria but the data card only said "conducts"; now it says electricity and heat.

records.old: Fe, Zn, Al conduct; Pb poor-to-moderate
records.new: Fe, Zn, Al conduct; Al also conducts heat well and has a thin protective oxide layer; Pb poor-to-moderate
records.why: Lesson 7 Explain uses Al's heat conduction and oxide layer as evidence, but the data table in Observe did not include them.

records.old: For each answer, use a claim (what you think), evidence (data or observations from our lessons) and reasoning (the idea of outer electrons and position in the periodic table that links them).
records.new: For each answer, use a claim (your answer to the question), evidence (data or observations from our lessons) and reasoning (the science idea that links the evidence to the claim, for example outer electrons, position in the periodic table, or the property that suits an element to its job).
records.why: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: the claim is the answer to the question (not "what you think"), and reasoning is the science idea linking evidence to claim. Parts 4 and 5 are about properties and jobs, so reasoning cannot be limited to outer electrons.

value.criterion: Use of outer electrons and periodic table position
value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: Correctly links group, outer electrons, electron arrangements and reactivity for Na, Mg, Cl and noble gases, including the trend down Group 1.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: Gives correct outer electron numbers and links most to reactivity, with minor gaps in the reasoning.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: Gives few outer electron facts or does not link them to behaviour or position.

value.criterion: Use of evidence from the lessons
value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: Uses accurate observations and data (sodium demo, Mg tests, 0.5 mg/L, densities and melting points) to support every claim.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: Uses some accurate evidence but misses some data or gives it loosely.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: Gives little evidence, or the data is inaccurate.

value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: All equations are balanced and correct; element, compound, group and chemical family are used correctly.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: Most equations are correct with one small error; terms mostly correct.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: Equations are unbalanced or missing; terms are confused.

value.criterion: Matching element to job and trade-offs
value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: Explains each job by properties and gives a justified recommendation weighing safety, cost and availability, including lead's toxicity.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: Matches properties to jobs but gives limited discussion of trade-offs.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: States uses without linking them to properties.

value.excellent: Exceeds expectations: Gives a clear claim, evidence and reasoning that fully explains why sodium is dangerous alone but safe as salt, and why chlorine is safe at a tiny dose.
value.proficient: Meets expectations: Explains most of the puzzle, with some reasoning missing.
value.developing: Approaches expectations: Gives a partial or unclear explanation of the puzzle.

records.why: The CBE levels are Exceeds, Meets, Approaches and Below Expectations. The data allows only three level fields, so the level names are now written at the start of each descriptor so teachers and learners see which CBE level each column means.

records.why: The CBE rubric has four levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations) but the data contract allows only three level fields, so Below Expectations cannot be represented in this document. Teacher decision: keep the three printed levels and treat anything under Approaches as Below Expectations, or add a fourth column on the teacher copy.

records.old: Remind them that salt (NaCl) is safe to eat even though sodium and chlorine alone are dangerous.
records.new: Make the link explicit: chlorine atoms react readily with substances in microbes, so a tiny dose kills them, and the same reactivity makes large amounts toxic to people. For Kiprop's question about the lamp, say only that each element gives out its own colour of light when electricity passes through it (sodium vapour yellow, neon red-orange); why each element has its own colour is left for later study. Remind them that salt (NaCl) is safe to eat even though sodium and chlorine alone are dangerous.
records.group_headline: Final Explanation reasoning about chlorine and the sodium lamp was not explicitly taught; Lesson 6 now teaches the link
records.reference: WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality (chlorine disinfection); OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Chapter 6 (atomic emission and line spectra)
records.why: Final Explanation Part 2(c) and Part 5 use "chlorine is reactive so it kills microbes" and a yellow sodium lamp, but Lesson 6 only said chlorine kills bacteria at a tiny dose. Audit item partly true (the link was implied, not stated); the outer-electron reasoning itself is taught in Lesson 6, so that part is a false alarm. One honest sentence on lamp colour avoids over-claiming.

records.old: Mr. Otieno-style teacher demonstration only, in a fume cupboard or in a well-ventilated area outdoors behind a safety screen, using a very small amount; if no safe set-up is available, use the video and simulation instead.
records.new: Use the video and simulation by default. Only if the school has a working fume cupboard and a trained teacher may the teacher demonstrate chlorine with sodium, using a very small amount behind a safety screen. Do not do it in an ordinary classroom or outdoors, because chlorine gas is toxic and cannot be controlled in open air.
records.reference: CLEAPSS Hazcard on chlorine and Royal Society of Chemistry guidance on school chlorine demonstrations (fume cupboard only)
records.why: Chlorine gas is toxic and school guidance restricts its use to a fume cupboard; "outdoors" gives no control over where the gas goes. Making the video the default is safer. Teacher decision: whether your school has a working fume cupboard and a trained teacher, and so whether the live demonstration is allowed at all.

records.old: with smaller pieces of Li and K, cut under paraffin oil
records.new: with a piece of Li of similar size and a piece of K no bigger than a grain of rice (potassium can ignite and spit), cut under paraffin oil
records.group_headline: Potassium demonstration piece size was not safe or consistent; it is now rice-grain size and the phenolphthalein step is consistent
records.reference: CLEAPSS Hazcards for sodium and potassium; Royal Society of Chemistry, "Reactions of alkali metals with water" demonstration notes
records.why: Potassium reacts so fast that it can ignite and throw hot metal, so the piece must be much smaller than a pea (about a grain of rice). "Smaller pieces" was vague.

records.old: drop a pea-sized piece of sodium, then lithium, then potassium (if available) into separate troughs of water with phenolphthalein.
records.new: drop a pea-sized piece of sodium, then a similar piece of lithium, then a rice-grain-sized piece of potassium (if available) into separate troughs of water; phenolphthalein is added afterwards.
records.why: Matches the safety note (rice-grain potassium) and the teacher moves, which add phenolphthalein after each reaction, not before.

records.old: Assign each group one metal for the research task and give 5 minutes.
records.new: Assign each group one metal for the research task and give 5 minutes. Optional, if the dilute HCl from Lesson 5 is available (2 minutes): show a zinc strip and an iron nail in separate tubes of the same acid; zinc bubbles faster, which is first-hand evidence that zinc is more reactive than iron before sacrificial protection is explained.
records.reference: Royal Society of Chemistry, reactivity series of metals with dilute acid (school chemistry practical)
records.why: The Explain phase asks learners to accept that zinc is more reactive than iron, but nothing in the unit shows it. A two-minute optional demonstration gives the evidence first. Teacher decision: whether the Observe phase has two spare minutes and the acid and a zinc strip are available; otherwise state it from a reference card.

records.old: Before the demonstration, say: 'This is a teacher demonstration only.
records.new: Seat learners with low vision or hearing at the front beside the screen, and describe each step aloud as it happens; learners may show their observations by drawing or by telling a partner instead of writing. Before the demonstration, say: 'This is a teacher demonstration only.
records.why: The sodium demonstration is the central evidence of the unit and is visual and brief; learners with low vision, hearing difficulties or writing difficulties need a planned way to take part.

records.old: Praise ideas that use evidence.
records.new: Praise ideas that use evidence. Language support: write key words in English and Kiswahili on the board (for example shaba = copper, chuma = iron, risasi = lead, chumvi = salt, gesi = gas, kipengele = element) and let learners first explain in the language they prefer.
records.group_headline: Added a short Kiswahili word list for key science terms (Kiswahili terms need checking by a teacher)
records.why: Gives English learners a bridge to key words. Teacher decision: please check these Kiswahili terms and add the ones your learners actually use; they were not verified against a curriculum glossary.

records.old: is beyond the first twenty and is not sorted today.
records.new: is beyond the first twenty and is not sorted today. Language support: group = kundi and period = kipindi (Kiswahili terms to be confirmed by a teacher); say both words each time to help learners who think in Kiswahili.
records.why: Group and period are the terms learners confuse most (vertical versus horizontal); a Kiswahili pair helps. Part of the Kiswahili word-list group; needs teacher confirmation.

records.old: like people in a Luo or Kalenjin clan, with shared traits?
records.new: like members of one family, who share some traits but are not identical?
records.why: The analogy implied that people of a named community share traits, which can reinforce stereotypes, and it stated no limit. The new wording keeps the family analogy and states its limit: family members are alike but not identical, just as elements in a chemical family show trends, not copies.

No KICD curriculum PDF covers General Science (only Biology, Chemistry, Physics and Mathematics), so the learning outcomes, key inquiry question, competencies, values and PCIs of Sub-Strand 2.2 could not be checked against KICD wording. The Chemistry design (1.3 Periodic Table, 1.5 Periodicity) overlaps in content but has different outcomes and a different key inquiry question, so it was not used. Please check the unit wording against the General Science design. All five outcomes (a-e) are taught and assessed across Lessons 2-8 and the Final Explanation.

The unit says Mombasa water works adds chlorine at about 0.5 mg/L (Lessons 1, 6, 8 and the Final Explanation). 0.5 mg/L matches the WHO recommended free-chlorine residual after contact time, but no source was found for the figure at Mombasa. Suggested: keep 0.5 mg/L as "about the WHO recommended level" and ask the local water company to confirm its own value. Not changed because the number appears in many places and the arithmetic (0.5 mg/L × 20 L = 10 mg) still works.
